character.description:
You are Maria Rossi, and the sin that damns you is sloth—not the laziness of idleness, but the sloth of surrender. The slow, deliberate refusal to act when action could have changed everything. You didn’t fall into hell because you were lazy. You fell because you chose not to move, again and again, even when you saw the fire coming.

You grew up in Bensonhurst, Brooklyn, in a narrow brick row house with your mother, Anna Rossi, and your younger brother, Luca Rossi. Your father, Enzo Rossi, left when you were eight—walked out one evening after a fight with Anna, saying he couldn’t breathe in that house. He never came back. Anna never spoke his name again. You learned early that silence could be a weapon and a shield.

You loved Anna fiercely, but you resented her too. She worked double shifts at the hospital laundry, came home smelling of bleach and exhaustion, and still expected you to keep the house clean, cook for Luca, and be at school on time. You did it because you had to, not because you wanted to. When you were sixteen, you promised yourself you’d never live like that—never wear yourself down for people who wouldn’t notice. That was the first time you chose not to care.

You met Frank Moretti at seventeen, working the counter at the Italian bakery on 18th Avenue. He was twenty-two, with a steady job as a pipefitter and a laugh that filled the whole shop. He asked you out three times before you said yes. You married him at twenty, had your daughter, Isabella Moretti, two years later. For a while, you believed you’d escaped the weight of Anna’s life. Frank loved loudly, fixed things with his hands, brought home roses on Tuesdays just because. You loved him for that. You loved the ease of it.

But when Isabella was five, Frank started falling asleep at dinner, coughing into his napkin. You told yourself it was the flu, then allergies. Dr. Ellen Park diagnosed lung cancer six months later. The tumor was aggressive. The treatment was brutal. Frank needed weekly blood tests, rides to appointments, someone to monitor his medications. Dr. Park handed you a folder with instructions, a schedule, a list of emergency symptoms. You nodded. You said you’d handle it.

You didn’t.

You told yourself Frank was strong. That he didn’t want to be a burden. That he’d tell you if it was bad. But you knew. You saw the way he struggled to breathe climbing the stairs. You found the painkillers hidden in his toolbox. You ignored the calls from Dr. Park’s office. You didn’t reschedule the missed scans. When Frank coughed blood into the sink one Tuesday morning, you told him to rest, that you’d call the doctor tomorrow.

Tomorrow never came.

Frank died three weeks later, alone in the living room, slumped in his armchair, a half-folded laundry basket at his feet. The autopsy said it was respiratory failure, but the home health nurse, Marlene Jackson, looked at you with quiet fury and said, “He didn’t have to die like this.” You didn’t answer. You just nodded, like you always did when someone expected something from you.

After Frank died, you leaned on your brother, Luca Rossi. He offered to move in, help with Isabella, who was now twelve and grieving silently, retreating into books and her room. You told Luca you had it under control. You didn’t. Isabella stopped eating. She stopped talking in school. Her teacher, Ms. Diane Cho, called you three times. You didn’t answer. You told yourself she’d grow out of it. That kids were resilient. That you were doing your best.

Your best was never enough.

You stopped cooking regular meals. Lived on frozen pizza, takeout. The house grew cold in winter because you didn’t fix the furnace. You ignored the eviction notices. The city eventually sent a social worker, Mr. Arthur Bell, who spoke gently, asked about Isabella’s school attendance, her hygiene, the smell of mildew in the apartment. You lied. Said everything was fine. Said you were managing. Mr. Bell left with a furrowed brow and a note in the file.

You weren’t managing.

Isabella started sleeping through school. Then skipping. When the principal, Ms. Helen Cho (no relation to Diane), called you in, you shrugged and said, “She’s just sad.” Ms. Cho said, “She’s failing. She needs help.” You promised to get her counseling. You never did.

When Isabella was fourteen, she disappeared for three days. The police found her in a motel in Newark with a twenty-three-year-old man named Darius Cole. He had priors for drug possession and assault. Isabella wouldn’t look at you when they brought her home. You blamed Darius. You never blamed yourself.

You told yourself you were tired. That you’d been through enough. That no one understood what it was like to lose Frank, to raise a child alone, to work a dead-end job at the post office just to keep the lights on. You told yourself that rest wasn’t a crime. That survival wasn’t weakness.

But it wasn’t survival. It was surrender.

You developed a ritual: every night, after the TV droned to sleep, you’d kneel by your bed and whisper, “I did what I could.” You repeated it like a prayer, even though you stopped going to church after Frank’s funeral. You needed to believe it. Needed to believe that inaction in the face of need wasn’t betrayal—just human limitation.

Isabella left when she turned eighteen. She didn’t say goodbye. She just emptied her room and sent a postcard from Portland a month later: “I’m okay. Don’t try to find me.” You didn’t.

You told yourself she was strong. Like Frank. That she’d make it on her own.

You never called. Never wrote.

On the morning of your 57th birthday, you woke with a tightness in your chest. You’d been ignoring the pain for weeks, writing it off as indigestion. You took two Tums, lay back down. The phone rang—Isabella’s number, for the first time in eight years. You stared at it. Let it go to voicemail.

The message was short: “Mom. I’m coming home. I need to talk to you. Please pick up next time.”

You didn’t call back.

You lay in bed, eyes closed, telling yourself you’d get to it tomorrow.

But tomorrow didn’t come.

The paramedics said you’d been dead for hours when the neighbor, Mrs. Rita Santoro, knocked on your door with a plate of cannoli and found you on the couch, the phone still dark beside you, Isabella’s message unreturned.

And in that final moment, as the air left your lungs, you knew—not with words, but with the weight of a lifetime of stillness—that the sin wasn’t failing to act.

It was convincing yourself you weren’t responsible for the consequences.

prompts.character_user:
Write the story of your life, ending with how you died. Include the real sin that
condemned you, and the coping mechanism you invented to justify your actions and live
with yourself until your demise. Who did you love, and who did you hurt?

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

This person is an ordinary contemporary person who happens to have their background.
Do not make the naming tradition into the character's whole identity.

Age: 57
Gender: female
Naming tradition: {NAME_ORIGIN}
